text: through him. “Yeah — hang on—” The flashlight slipped as he tried to pull it free, fingers fumbling, nerves not quite obeying. He caught it on the second grab and thumbed it on. The beam sputtered. Then held. Barely. It cast a cone of weak yellow light maybe a foot and a half ahead — just enough to see David’s outline, slick with water and tension. The shadows pressed in thick around the edges, greedy and reluctant to let anything through. “Better than nothing,” he rubbed at his shoulder where he had caught it in the dark. “Goddamn lockers.” David turned toward the barricade, the light barely outlining the mess of desks and shelves still wedged into the stairwell. “I’m not wandering blind,” he said. “I’m gonna try moving this crap again. Just one desk. Just one fucking desk and I can climb over the rest.” He planted his feet in the water and shoved. The stack shifted and resettled. He shoved again. Same result. He worked his way along the pile, trying different points of leverage, each impact swallowed before it could properly echo, the sounds dying the moment they left his hands like they were ashamed of themselves. He very pointedly did not say anything about that. “Fuck’s sake.” He stepped back, kicked a locker. The metal thunk was dull. Muffled. Like it had been swallowed by insulation. Dwight barely heard it. He was inching along the wall again, one hand trailing rust-damp metal as he backtracked toward the pipe hallway. The flashlight shivered in his grip as he swept it across the darkness. He turned, slipping slightly as the water surged with his motion. He nearly dropped the flashlight. Caught it with both hands and steadied his breath. David had both hands locked on a locker handle now, wrenching hard. Something groaned behind it but didn’t give. “Why can’t I hear anything?” David muttered. “I’m making noise, I know I am.” Dwight didn’t answer. He was still staring at the water. The whole basement was dark, sure — but the water was darker, somehow. Not just murky. The light caught the surface and went nowhere, reflected back like the water had decided it wasn't interested in being seen through. Something grazed his shin. He flinched hard, flashlight jerking up and sending spastic light darts along the ceiling. He spun in place slowly, sweeping the beam down again. It barely cut the surface, but it was darker than it should have been. Murkier. It wasn’t just dirty — it was opaque, metallic, like it had decided reflection was another way out and sealed it. Like more than just rust was bleeding through the pipes. Nothing there. Obviously, nothing there. The water found his calves while he was still trying to convince himself of that. The beam barely penetrated an inch before giving up entirely, which was either a property of the water or a property of the flashlight, and he wasn't sure which option was worse. The Nothing bumped his calf. Gentle. Almost curious. His breath hitched. “David?” David didn’t look up. He had both hands on a large desk, hauling upward with everything he had. The desk rocked — genuinely rocked this time, a real shift, the stack above it grinding with what sounded almost like progress — and then slid smoothly back into place as if he'd never touched it. “David, I think there’s something in the water,” Dwight whispered. David glanced back, shadowed eyes narrow. “Debris. Keep your head.” David gave the desk another shove. It rocked, then slid back into place as if correcting itself. “Debris doesn’t do that.” "I've nearly got it." He didn't have it. Dwight could see that plainly. But David's jaw was set in the particular way it got when he'd decided something was happening through sheer force of will, and interrupting that with there might be something in the water with us was not a conversation Dwight felt equipped to have right now. David simply shoved the barricade again, muscles bunching under soaked cloth. Another scrape, another futile give. The water rippled outward and came back against them both. The water had reached his knees at some point without Dwight noticing, the warmth of it creeping upward so gradually that his body had simply accepted it. Something grazed the inside of his knee — higher than before — and he locked every muscle in his body simultaneously, the flashlight beam skittering sideways as his hand jerked. Nothing. Dark water. Pipes. His own heartbeat loud enough to hear. Minutes — maybe longer — passed in the churn of their own breathing. The beam quivered between them like a nervous heartbeat. Then the furniture groaned. A shelf slid down from the top of the pile and hit the water without a splash. The air absorbed the sound. — The water was up to their waists when David finally gave up on the stairwell. The stack above David shifted, and a cascade of debris came down to fill the gap he'd made. He stepped back, breathing hard, and looked at his hands. Knuckles scraped raw. His shoulder had graduated from bruised to something more insistent. The stairwell stared back at him, unchanged and utterly indifferent to everything he'd put into it. A shelf tumbled down from the plug and landed with a wet thud, nearly hitting him. "It’s not giving," he spat, kicking one of the desks hard enough to jar his shin. Dwight’s light jittered across the walls. He tried not to look at the water anymore. He didn’t want to see it. “We should go back. Try the first stairs. At least those were open.” “Are you sure he’s moved on?” “No...” Dwight cast the beam into the pipe hall for a moment, shuddering lightly at the way the light seemed to be eaten in the distance. “But it’s not like we can just stay here.” David gave a long, ragged sigh, finally stepping back from the mass of furniture
